headline: ETH Zürich and Huawei Research measured what in-DRAM computing actually costs and found the bit-layout conversion, not the arithmetic, dominates: it takes 77 to 100 percent of the run time in the three of twelve workloads with the lowest operations per byte.

items.title: Charge in an oxide replaces the implanted junction, and gain goes on top
items.dek: Hele Savin's group, which published the original induced-junction black silicon photodiode in 2016, has now built one that avalanches — a detector whose junction comes from fixed charge in an alumina film rather than from implanted dopants, reaching gains of roughly 4 to 23.
items.why_it_matters: An implanted or diffused emitter puts a dead layer exactly where ultraviolet light is absorbed, so the carriers it frees recombine before anything collects them, and that is why ordinary silicon photodiodes give up most of their response below 400 nanometres. Inducing the junction with a charged oxide removes that layer, which lets the detector keep the one property ultraviolet silicon has always had and nobody could reach: in the ultraviolet a single absorbed photon can free more than one electron–hole pair, so quantum efficiency exceeds 100 percent before any multiplication is applied. Avalanche gain then multiplies a number that already started above one.
items.background_md: A photodiode's external quantum efficiency is carriers delivered per incident photon, and two things cap it. Photons reflected off the surface never enter at all; carriers generated within a few tens of nanometres of the surface recombine before they reach the junction. Ultraviolet light is absorbed almost entirely inside that surface region, so it suffers both losses at once. Black silicon — a dense forest of needles etched into the wafer — attacks the first by making the refractive index change gradually over a wavelength instead of abruptly at a plane. The second is decided by how the junction itself is made.
items.deeper_md:
The reported device holds external quantum efficiency above 100% across 200–400 nm with a peak near 130%, and 92–100% from 400 to 700 nm, with avalanche gain of roughly 4 to 23 depending on bias and dark current in the picoampere range up to 80 V before it climbs towards breakdown. No ion implantation is involved: an atomic-layer-deposited aluminium oxide film carries a large negative fixed charge, and that charge inverts the silicon beneath it into a collecting layer. The same approach in the group's 2016 Nature Photonics device held efficiency above 96% from 250 to 950 nm with an inversion layer reaching about 30 µm into the substrate, and its 2020 Physical Review Letters follow-up certified above 130% in the ultraviolet with no external amplification at all, attributing the excess to impact ionisation inside the nanostructures.

Two things to hold. The above-unity figures are quantum yield rather than gain — a property of silicon at ultraviolet photon energies that does not extend to visible or infrared light, where this device reports 92–100% and not more. And the certified 130% was measured on a diode with no avalanche region, where a metrology laboratory can calibrate against a reference detector; a device whose gain depends on bias is a considerably harder thing to certify, and this preprint is days old with no independent measurement.

glossary.definition: Charge carriers delivered by the detector per photon arriving at it. Above 100% means at least some photons freed more than one electron–hole pair.
A junction formed by the electric field of fixed charge trapped in an overlying dielectric, which inverts the semiconductor underneath, rather than by implanting or diffusing dopants into it.
The factor by which one photogenerated carrier is multiplied when the field is high enough that carriers knock further carriers out of the lattice on their way across.
A carrier with enough kinetic energy giving that energy to a bound electron and lifting it across the bandgap, creating a second electron–hole pair from one.

items.fab_angle: The electrically active layer here is a deposition and a trapped charge rather than a dopant profile, which removes the implanter — the tool a university cleanroom is least likely to own — from the flow for this device. What it puts in its place is a film whose fixed charge density has to be reproducible, so the control problem moves from dose and anneal to deposition chemistry and interface quality.

items.title: Which layer sits in the middle changes the field that switches the stack
items.dek: Alireza Sepehrinezhad and six co-authors ran reactive molecular dynamics on sandwiches of zinc oxide and magnesium-alloyed zinc oxide — wurtzite ferroelectrics, which store a bit by pushing whole atoms through the crystal — and report that a switchable neighbour cuts the field zinc oxide needs by up to fivefold.
items.why_it_matters: Wurtzite ferroelectrics are the only ferroelectric family a nitride or oxide semiconductor line already knows how to deposit, and their standing problem is that the field which reverses polarisation sits uncomfortably close to the field that destroys the film: aluminium scandium nitride, the benchmark, needs above 3 megavolts per centimetre and is driven at fields approaching ten. Anything that lowers the switching field without giving up stored polarisation widens that gap directly. What this work adds is that part of the lever is geometry rather than chemistry — the same two materials in the same proportions switched at different fields depending on which one was in the middle, at every temperature examined.
items.background_md: A ferroelectric stores a bit as the direction of a permanent electric polarisation and reverses it by moving atoms, not charge. In the wurtzite family — aluminium nitride, zinc oxide and their alloys — reversal means dragging the entire cation sublattice through the plane of its nitrogen or oxygen neighbours, a large atomic displacement that therefore needs a large field. That is the family's defining trade: remanent polarisation of order 100 microcoulombs per square centimetre, far above the conventional perovskite oxides, bought at coercive fields measured in megavolts per centimetre, which is close to where the film simply breaks down.
items.deeper_md:
The simulations are ReaxFF molecular dynamics on ZnO/Zn₁₋ₓMgₓO/ZnO and Zn₁₋ₓMgₓO/ZnO/Zn₁₋ₓMgₓO trilayers, started pristine and single-domain. Coupling zinc oxide to a switchable magnesium-alloyed neighbour lowers the field needed to reverse it by up to fivefold. Temperature generally lowers the coercive field, while magnesium content does not — its effect is non-monotonic. At equal proportions of the two materials, stacks with ZnO at the centre switched at lower fields than stacks with the alloy at the centre, at all four temperatures examined, and layer-resolved trajectories show normal stress redistributing near the heterointerfaces in a direction-dependent way, which the authors read as a stress-assisted cooperative pathway. Thick magnesium-rich stacks instead switch in steps or get stuck in a low-polarity state.

What to hold against it. These are fixed-charge atomistic simulations with electron microscopy supplying structural context only, so no coercive field is quoted in volts per centimetre against a measured device, and fivefold is a ratio between simulated stacks rather than between fabricated ones. A different group's preprint ten days earlier, using the same reactive-MD approach on the same material system, puts the achievable reduction nearer 50% and attributes most of it to charge redistribution at the head of the advancing switching filament rather than to strain — so the mechanism is contested inside the same method, not only across methods.

glossary.definition: The applied field at which polarisation reverses. In wurtzite ferroelectrics it runs to megavolts per centimetre, within a small factor of the field that breaks the dielectric down.

The hexagonal crystal structure of aluminium nitride, gallium nitride and zinc oxide. It is polar along its c axis, so the crystal carries a built-in polarisation whose sign depends on which way the cation sits.
The polarisation still present once the applied field is removed; it is the quantity a memory cell actually reads out, and it sets the charge available per bit.

A reactive force field — an empirical interatomic potential fitted to quantum calculations that lets bonds break and re-form, so the simulation can follow a switching event that fixed-bond molecular dynamics cannot.

items.title: In-DRAM compute spends most of its time rearranging bits, not computing
items.dek: Nine researchers at ETH Zürich and Huawei Research Zürich measured what computing inside a DRAM chip actually costs, and found the rearranging dominates: turning data sideways so one number's bits run down a column instead of across a cache line takes 77 to 100 percent of the run time in three of twelve workloads.
items.why_it_matters: Computing in a DRAM array gets its speed from the sense amplifiers — activate several rows at once and the charge sharing settles to their majority value, which is one bitwise operation on every column of the row simultaneously. Arithmetic done that way needs each number's bits stacked vertically down a column, and every processor in the world stores them horizontally along a cache line, so a layout conversion is the price of admission; the paper puts that price at 3.9× in performance and 3.7× in energy efficiency. Removing it turns out not to require touching the array at all — reordering the bits inside each memory request at the controller is enough.
items.background_md: Moving a word of data from DRAM to a processor costs far more energy than the arithmetic performed on it, which is the entire argument for doing the arithmetic in the memory array instead. A DRAM row is read by dumping thousands of capacitors onto their bit lines at once; drive two or three rows together and the shared charge settles to the majority value, so the array has computed a logic function on thousands of bits in the time of one access. Everything built on this is bit-serial — the array works on one bit position of every number at a time — which is what fixes how the numbers must be laid out.
items.deeper_md:
PipeDRAM's mechanism is a deterministic permutation applied in the memory controller: each scalar stays within a single DRAM chip, but its bit positions are spread across that chip's mats, so a horizontally laid-out cache line arrives already in a workable arrangement. Each mat then becomes a pipeline stage handling one bit position, converting mat-level parallelism into pipeline parallelism under a modulo schedule computed offline. Against three prior processing-using-DRAM designs it reports 11.8×, 11.8× and 80.4× higher performance and 25.4×, 3.0× and 38.0× lower energy, and against conventional hardware 356× and 11.7× the energy efficiency of a CPU and a GPU averaged over twelve real applications, for 1.86% area on the DRAM die and 0.05% on the CPU.

The paper is honest about what the pipeline costs: it runs on 32× fewer SIMD lanes than the transposed layout would give, the hierarchical copy scheme that keeps it fed uses 2.2× the energy of the simpler variant, and there are fill and drain phases before steady state. The larger caveat belongs to the whole field — this is a cycle-level simulation of a modified DRAM chip, and the multi-row activation it assumes sits outside manufacturer timing specifications. A 2023 study of 120 off-the-shelf DDR4 chips from two manufacturers did get up to 32 rows to activate together, but only by replicating input data to raise the success rate, and it reports success rates rather than guarantees.

glossary.definition: Computing with the memory array's own analogue behaviour — charge sharing between simultaneously activated rows — rather than with logic added next to the array.
The smallest tile a DRAM array is divided into, with its own sense amplifiers. A chip holds many, and they can be driven independently, which is where the parallelism in this design comes from.
Storing one number's bits down a single column so that one row operation processes the same bit position of thousands of numbers at once; the opposite of the horizontal cache-line layout a CPU uses.
Operations performed per byte of data moved. Below roughly 10 the workload is limited by data movement rather than arithmetic, which is exactly where the transposition cost swallows everything.

items.fab_angle: 1.86% of a DRAM die is the number to argue about. DRAM is sold on cost per bit and its array efficiency is guarded to a fraction of a percent, so a change that spends nearly two percent of the die on logic has to be justified against the same area filled with cells — which is the reason proposals of this kind keep being evaluated on unmodified commodity parts instead.

items.title: A circuit switch in front of the switch chips buys their lost ports back
items.dek: Three researchers at ETH Zürich and one at Microsoft Research put a circuit switch in front of a pair of Ethernet switch chips and remap which chip each incoming port lands on as traffic shifts, so most packets never have to cross between the two chips at all.
items.why_it_matters: A switch chip has run out of die — the reticle caps its area, and the industry's answer of gluing several chips together immediately spends the ports it gained on links between them. Underprovision those internal links and the paper measures up to 4× lower throughput and a 9× worse tail flow completion time; provision them fully and the ports are gone anyway. Fixing the egress side and letting only ingress ports move is what makes the placement tractable: it collapses balanced graph partitioning, which is NP-hard, into a linear assignment the Hungarian algorithm solves exactly, and that is the reason the mapping can be recomputed while the switch is running.
items.background_md: An Ethernet switch chip is among the largest digital dies anyone builds, and what it sells is radix — how many ports it terminates — multiplied by the rate of each. Both are limited by area: serialiser-deserialiser blocks and packet buffers do not shrink with the logic around them, and no single die can exceed the reticle field. The standard escape is to build a chassis from several chips wired into a small internal network. That works, with one structural cost: every port spent on the internal network is a port the customer never sees.
items.deeper_md:
The indirection layer is circuit-switched, so it makes no per-packet decisions — only a periodic remapping of ingress ports onto ASICs from port-level statistics, collected in Θ(pn) and solved with a greedy heuristic in Θ(pn log pn). The paper claims about 30% more bandwidth and radix from the same chips than a state-of-the-art non-blocking multi-ASIC design, which in a two-layer fat tree is 30–78% more hosts and in a three-layer one 49–138%. The prototype is two Tofino switches, one emulating a two-ASIC packet switch and the other the circuit switch, with eight hosts at 100 Gb/s each and 2:1 oversubscription; fine-tuning Llama 3.2 3B across eight RTX 4000 Ada GPUs with PyTorch FSDP gives 3× the token throughput of the comparison architectures, with inter-ASIC link utilisation near zero.

The authors state the limits themselves. The benefit lives in the two-to-four-ASIC regime and decays past it, because each port can be assigned to exactly one chip and everything else still has to cross. And the scheme assumes traffic is stable over a reconfiguration interval, which the repeating collectives of a training job satisfy and a general datacentre mix may not. The motivating observation is a cadence rather than a law: Broadcom shipped a new Tomahawk generation every two years up to Tomahawk 4, and has taken three years for each of the two since.

glossary.definition: The number of ports a switch terminates. Radix and per-port rate are what a switch chip sells, and radix sets how many hosts a fat tree of a given depth can reach.
Setting up a fixed path that carries everything sent into it until it is torn down, with no per-packet lookup. Cheap and fast in hardware, but it cannot react inside the time of a packet.
The ratio between the traffic that can arrive at a stage and the capacity leaving it. 2:1 means the internal links can carry only half of what the ports can deliver.
How long the slowest flows take to finish, rather than the average. In a collective operation the tail is what decides when every participant can move on.

items.title: Consensus fast paths, derived from the latencies instead of invented
items.dek: Clément Burgelin and four co-authors reframed the shortcut that lets a geo-replicated database commit in one network round trip: instead of designing yet another protocol by hand, they state the condition any such shortcut must satisfy and then solve for the fastest arrangement that satisfies it.
items.why_it_matters: Every replicated system in production runs a fast path whose quorum sizes were picked by hand for one assumed topology, and they are not interchangeable. Fast Paxos needs a quorum larger than (n+f)/2 because it has no second round in which to spread evidence around; Egalitarian Paxos gets away with a smaller one by letting a proposer also act as an acceptor, which manufactures witnesses outside the quorum intersection. Which of them is fastest depends on where the replicas physically sit. Turning the choice into an optimisation means the protocol follows from the measured round-trip times rather than from a menu — and it is derived rather than argued, which matters in a corner of the literature where the hand-written arguments have had bugs in them.
items.background_md: Replicating a database across continents means agreeing on an order of operations with no shared clock, and the classic answer routes every request through one elected leader — two network round trips for anyone not sitting beside that leader, which across an ocean is nearly everyone. A fast path is the optimisation that commits in a single round trip when nothing goes wrong. It is not free: with no second round available to reconcile a disagreement, any two quorums that could have accepted different values must overlap in enough processes that a recovering replica can still work out which value was chosen.
items.deeper_md:
The condition the paper extracts is about the spread of knowledge rather than intersection alone: for any two proposers, their requirements together must force at least f+1 processes to have witnessed an acceptance by some process in the intersection of their quorums, and separately every quorum must hold more than f processes. Existing protocols then fall out as points in that space — Fast Paxos with q > (n+f)/2, which is six of seven processes at n=7, f=3; EPaxos with five, because a proposer that is also an acceptor can create witnesses outside the intersection; SwiftPaxos with a single shared quorum of f+1. KCensus turns the condition into a minimisation of expected latency weighted by each process's probability of proposing, prunes the search to about ten candidate budgets per proposer across 31 AWS replicas, and reports up to 16% lower average latency than the best prior protocol in a geo-replicated key-value store.

The assumptions are load-bearing and the authors list them: fixed and known network latencies, crash faults with perfect failure detection, contention-free execution, and one latency metric at a time — it cannot optimise the mean and the 99th percentile together, and they note that the best prior protocol differs between metrics and deployments. As for why derivation is worth having, an OPODIS 2025 paper reports that EPaxos itself, the most-copied protocol in this family, is ambiguously specified and carries non-trivial bugs.

glossary.definition: A set of replicas large enough that any two such sets share members, which is what stops two proposals being committed in ignorance of one another.
f is how many simultaneous crashes the protocol survives; n is the replica count. Classical leaderless consensus needs n = 2f+1 to keep making progress.
The code path that commits in one network round trip when there are no failures and no conflicting proposals. A slower path exists to clean up whenever that assumption breaks.
A process that has seen some replica accept a value. Recovery after a crash works by collecting enough witnesses to conclude which value could possibly have been committed.

items.title: Bits for the state should follow how long an error survives in it
items.dek: Hongren Chen and Jiayang He show that the fixed-size recurrent state that replaces the key-value cache in hybrid language models survives being squeezed to about four bits per element, provided each row of the state is weighted by how long an error injected into it lasts before the model's own decay forgets it.
items.why_it_matters: Attention's memory grows with every token; the linear-attention layers now mixed into production models replace it with a state of fixed size, which is the whole reason for using them. But that state is read and written back on every single token, so a quantisation error is re-read and re-decayed rather than consumed once and discarded, and rows with slow decay accumulate errors that fast rows would have forgiven. The observability Gramian is the linear-systems quantity that says which rows are which, so allocating bits by it instead of uniformly is what makes four bits survivable where eight had been the working floor.
items.background_md: A transformer remembers by keeping every past key and value, so its memory grows linearly with context length and rereading it comes to dominate inference at long context. Linear-attention and state-space layers replace that with a fixed-size matrix updated once per token: each step multiplies the state by a diagonal decay and adds a rank-one write. Memory then stops growing with context, at the price of being lossy — old information fades at a rate the model learns separately for each channel. Production models now interleave both kinds of layer, so both kinds of memory sit in the same network.
items.deeper_md:
The state update is `S_t = (I − k_t a_tᵀ) D_t S_{t−1} + k_t (w_t ⊙ v_t)ᵀ`, with `D_t` a per-token diagonal decay. Because each row's decay rate sets how long an error injected there persists, the authors take distortion weights from the observability Gramian, normalise state ranges within each output-normalisation group so a fast-decaying row is not merely mistaken for a small one, and quantise the decay rates log-uniformly — a rate error Δs changes the retained signal by e^(−Δs/s), so a linear grid misspends its levels. No calibration data, rotation or retraining is required. At a four-bit mean payload with per-token quantisation, excess negative log-likelihood falls by 3.3×, 4.8× and 27.9× against the best of seven baselines on three hybrid models; at six bits the gap to a full-precision state is under 0.005 nats, which is about half a percent in perplexity.

The paper's own table is the caveat and it is unusually blunt. Across fifteen model–budget pairs the method is best in four, tied in seven and worse in four; at a two-bit mean on one model nine of the baselines beat it, and a long-context retrieval probe loses 0.10 against full precision on multi-value queries. It is a nine-page ICASSP 2027 submission, unrefereed, reporting distortion and likelihood rather than any measured throughput, so the claim is about how much information a given number of bits keeps, not about how fast it runs.

glossary.definition: The fixed-size matrix a linear-attention layer carries from one token to the next in place of a growing key–value cache; its size does not depend on how long the context is.
A linear-systems matrix measuring how strongly a disturbance of the state shows up in later outputs — large along slowly decaying directions, small along quickly decaying ones.
The natural-logarithm unit of a language model's loss. A gap of 0.005 nats corresponds to a perplexity ratio of about 1.005, so roughly half a percent.
The average number of bits spent per element of the state once mixed-precision allocation has finished; individual rows receive more or fewer than the mean.

foundations.subtitle: Every wire in every chip is grown upward from the floor of a trench, by an additive that speeds deposition up exactly where it piles up.
foundations.tldr: Copper cannot be plasma-etched into wires the way aluminium can, so the industry inverted the process: cut the trench into the insulator first, fill it with electroplated copper, then polish the excess away. Filling a submicron trench out of a solution ought to close the mouth before the floor is full and leave a void running down the middle of the wire, and the reason it does not is one organic additive that accumulates on the shrinking interface at the bottom and accelerates deposition wherever its coverage is highest.

sections.heading: Copper does not etch, so the process runs backwards
sections.body_md:
Aluminium wiring was made subtractively, and the sequence is the one everybody learns first: deposit a blanket metal film, print resist on top of it, plasma-etch the metal you do not want, then backfill the gaps with insulator. That works because aluminium's reaction products with chlorine chemistry leave the wafer as a gas. Copper has no equivalent — it forms no etch product volatile enough at wafer temperature for a plasma to carry away — so the subtractive flow has no exit for the material it removes.

The industry wanted copper anyway, because it conducts better than aluminium and resists electromigration better, which together decide how fast a wire can be and how long it lives. The answer was to reverse the order of operations. Pattern and etch the *dielectric*, producing empty trenches and holes; deposit a diffusion barrier and a thin copper seed to conduct the plating current; electroplate copper until everything is buried under a continuous overburden; then planarise the overburden away, leaving metal only where the trench was. The name is damascene, after the inlay technique, and inlay is exactly what it is.

sections.heading: Why filling a trench from a solution should fail
sections.body_md:
Think about what deposition does to a trench cross-section. If metal grows at the same rate on every exposed surface — conformal deposition — the two sidewalls advance toward each other while the floor advances upward, and the sidewalls have less distance to cover. They meet first. What you are left with is a seam running the length of the wire, and at best a weak line of grain boundaries, at worst an open circuit.

Reality is usually worse than conformal, because transport of copper ions to the mouth of the feature is easier than transport to its floor, so unaided plating is faster at the top. That pinches the opening shut early and traps a void in the middle. The features that matter here are not gentle: the NIST work that pinned down the mechanism was run in trenches 500 nm deep and 500 down to 90 nm wide, an aspect ratio past five to one at the narrow end. And a void is not a cosmetic defect in a wire that will carry current for ten years — it is where current crowds and where electromigration starts.

Superfill, or superconformal deposition, is the name for the opposite behaviour: growth that starts at the floor, moves upward faster than the sidewalls close, and leaves no seam at all.

sections.heading: Three additives, and the one that does the work
sections.body_md:
The bath is unglamorous: acid copper sulfate, plus chloride, plus two organic additives. In the NIST formulation those are polyethylene glycol and 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate. Polyethylene glycol, working together with chloride, adsorbs as a blocking film that raises the overpotential needed to deposit and therefore slows deposition down — it is the suppressor. The sulfonate displaces that film locally and lets deposition run fast again — it is the accelerator. Production baths add a third, a leveler, whose job is to knock down the bump of overplate that superfill leaves standing above a filled feature.

The experiment that shows this is a system rather than a list: leaving any of the three components out of the electrolyte produced voids at the centres of the trenches. The same optimised bath also shows hysteresis in its current–voltage curve — sweep the potential up and back down and the two branches do not coincide — and that hysteresis is the practical handle a fab uses to monitor whether its additives are still healthy, because additives break down and get dragged out with the wafers.

sections.heading: The trick is geometric: accelerator on a shrinking surface
sections.body_md:
The mechanism was named in 2001 and it is worth stating exactly, because the obvious explanations are wrong. It is not that more accelerator diffuses to the bottom of the trench. The statement is that the local growth velocity increases with the *coverage* of an adsorbed catalytic species on the copper–electrolyte interface — and that the species is not consumed and does not desorb. It floats on the metal surface as that surface advances.

Now watch a trench fill. The floor advances upward, and its area barely changes. But the concave corners where floor meets sidewall are advancing into a shrinking area, and the adsorbed accelerator riding on them has nowhere to go, so its coverage per unit area rises. Higher coverage means faster growth; faster growth into a concave corner shrinks the area further; coverage rises again. That positive feedback, running along the bottom of the feature, is what outruns the closing sidewalls. Because the driver is the change in interfacial area, and area change is set by curvature, the mechanism is called curvature-enhanced accelerator coverage. For dilute catalyst in features 350 to 100 nm wide, this area-change term, not accumulation out of the electrolyte, is what dominates.

sections.heading: What the model predicts that intuition does not
sections.body_md:
A mechanism that is fundamentally geometric has to be sensitive to geometry, and the useful predictions are the ones that follow from that. Josell, Wheeler and Moffat used the model to ask about vias rather than trenches and found that superconformal filling of a via is expected over a *narrower* range of plating conditions than a trench of the same aspect ratio. The reason is in the shape: a trench closes in one dimension while a via closes in two, so the interfacial area at the bottom of a via changes differently as it advances, and the feedback that makes superfill work is tuned differently. The consequence lands directly on dual damascene, where a via and the trench above it are filled in a single plating step and therefore have to share one process window.

Making that computable took another step. The 2003 treatment tracks the interface as the zero level set of a continuous scalar field, which gives curvature for free at every point and lets accelerator coverage be updated from it. Superfill stopped being something you found by sweeping additive concentrations and became something you could simulate before the bath was mixed.

sections.heading: After the plating: the film keeps changing, and the wire keeps getting worse
sections.body_md:
Plated copper does not stay as deposited. Films grown from the superfilling electrolyte recrystallise spontaneously at room temperature, and their resistivity falls by 23% within a few hours of coming out of the bath. That is a measurement trap worth internalising: a sheet-resistance number taken straight off the plating tool is describing a film that no longer exists by the time the wafer reaches the next step. Then the overburden has to come off, which is why damascene and chemical mechanical planarisation arrived as a pair — the inlay is only an inlay once the excess is polished away.

The long-run problem is not the plating. It is that copper stops behaving like copper when the wire gets thin: electrons scatter off grain boundaries and off the trench walls, and the diffusion barrier that keeps copper out of the silicon eats a fixed thickness from a shrinking cross-section, so resistivity climbs steeply as dimensions fall. That climb is now the thing interconnect research is organised around — the 2026 screening study cited below is combing through topological semimetals looking for surface states that still conduct at sizes where copper has given up.

glossary.definition: Patterning the dielectric rather than the metal: etch a trench, fill it with metal, polish the excess off. Named after the inlay technique, and adopted because copper cannot be plasma-etched.

Forming the via down to the layer below and the trench for the wire above in the dielectric first, then filling both in one metal deposition — fewer steps, but one plating process window has to serve two different geometries.
Deposition that is faster at the bottom of a feature than on its sidewalls, so the feature fills from the floor upward and closes without a seam or a void. The opposite of what unaided plating does.

The three organic additives in a damascene bath. The suppressor (with chloride) adsorbs as a blocking film and slows deposition everywhere; the accelerator displaces it and speeds deposition where it accumulates; the leveler flattens the overplate bump left above a filled feature.

The mechanism behind superfill: adsorbed accelerator is conserved on the advancing metal surface, so its coverage per unit area rises wherever that surface is shrinking — at concave corners — and higher coverage means faster local growth.
The continuous copper layer left above the wafer surface once every trench is full. It is deposited on purpose, because you cannot stop plating exactly at the trench top, and it is removed by CMP.

A thin conductive copper film deposited over the barrier before plating, because electroplating needs a conducting surface to carry current. Its continuity over the sidewalls of a high-aspect-ratio feature is a separate hard problem from the fill itself.

Room-temperature recrystallisation of as-plated copper, which drops resistivity by about a fifth over a few hours with no heat applied — so an electrical measurement made immediately after plating is not the film's final value.

foundations.try_this: Turn the self-annealing result into a measurement you own. Sputter a thin copper seed onto a blank test substrate, then plate it in a beaker of acid copper sulfate at a current density you have chosen and written down — a bench supply in constant-current mode and a copper anode is the whole rig. Pull the sample out, rinse it, and measure sheet resistance on the four-point probe immediately, then again at 30 minutes, 1, 2, 4 and 24 hours, keeping the probe spacing and the sample temperature fixed. Plot resistance against time on a log axis. A plain additive-free bath will not necessarily give you the 23% drop the NIST paper reports for its superfilling electrolyte, and that is the interesting part: whatever curve you get is a statement about the grain structure your bath produced, and it tells you how long a plated film has to sit before an electrical measurement of it means anything.
